items.title: Figure 1 caption question: A diagram shows two sealed samples of helium gas. Sample X is at 250 K and sample Y is at 400 K. Small arrows are drawn on some of the particles. What do the arrows represent, and in which sample are they longer?

body.html: Particles in a gas move randomly. Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles, 𝐾𝐸=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup>

Each arrow is a velocity vector of one gas particle: its length shows the speed and its direction shows the direction of motion. The helium atoms are identical, so a higher average kinetic energy means a higher average speed. Sample Y is hotter (400 K > 250 K), so its particles have the greater average kinetic energy and speeds, and its arrows are longer.

answer.html: The arrows are velocity vectors of the gas particles (length = speed). They are longer in sample Y (400 K) because the hotter gas has the higher average kinetic energy, so its particles move faster.

check.html: Sample X, being colder, has particles that strike the container walls more gently, so it would produce less pressure if the volumes were equal.

items.title: Get It? (thermal equilibrium): Give an everyday example of an object and its surroundings moving toward thermal equilibrium that does not involve anything being heated.

body.html: Thermal energy flows spontaneously from hot to cold until the temperatures match, and it can go either way depending on which object is hotter.

Choose an object that is colder than its surroundings. A can of soda taken out of the refrigerator and left on a kitchen counter warms: the room's more energetic air particles collide with the can and transfer energy to it. The can stops warming when it reaches room temperature.

answer.html: Example: a cold soda can on a kitchen counter. Thermal energy flows from the warmer room into the can until the can and the room are at the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

check.html: The colder object warms and the warmer surroundings cool slightly, never the reverse.

items.title: Figure 5 caption question: A liquid crystal strip is stuck to the glass wall of a fish tank to monitor the water. Summarize what happens from the moment the strip is attached until it gives a reading.

body.html: Conduction and thermal equilibrium (a thermometer reads its own temperature).

The strip starts at room temperature and the water is at a different temperature, so energy is conducted through the glass until the strip and the water are at the same temperature (thermal equilibrium). At that temperature the liquid-crystal molecules are arranged in a way that reflects a particular color, so the color tells the temperature. Until equilibrium is reached, the strip reads its own temperature, not the water's.

answer.html: Thermal energy is conducted between the water and the strip (through the glass) until the two reach thermal equilibrium; the liquid crystals show the color that matches that temperature, giving the reading.

check.html: The reading is only valid after waiting for equilibrium, which is why a thermometer should be left in place for a few moments.

items.title: Get It? (alcohol thermometer): A window thermometer uses red-dyed alcohol in a thin tube. When it is carried from a cold porch to a warm room, the column rises. Explain why.

body.html: A thermometer uses a property that changes with temperature (here, volume of a liquid).

In the warm room, thermal energy flows from the air to the bulb until the alcohol is at room temperature. The alcohol particles gain kinetic energy and move farther apart on average, so the liquid expands. Because the tube is narrow, the extra volume pushes the column up a long way, and the height at equilibrium is read against the scale.

answer.html: The alcohol warms to the room's temperature (thermal equilibrium), its particles move faster and spread out, so the liquid expands and rises in the narrow tube. The final height shows the temperature.

check.html: Carried back outside, the alcohol would cool and contract and the column would drop.

items.title: Get It? (absolute zero): A friend says that a freezer in the lab could reach −300°C. Use the idea of kinetic energy to explain why this is impossible.

body.html: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles; the Kelvin scale starts where this energy is zero, at 0 K = −273.15°C.
Convert the claim to kelvins using 𝑇<sub>𝐾</sub>= 𝑇<sub>𝐶</sub>+ 273.
A negative Kelvin temperature would mean a negative average kinetic energy, which is impossible because <sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> ≥0.

answer.html: It is impossible. The lowest possible temperature is absolute zero, −273.15°C (0 K), where the particles have no kinetic energy left to give up. −300°C would be below 0 K.

check.html: −300°C is colder than −273°C, so it is below the lowest possible temperature.

items.title: Figure 8 caption question: List one example each of conduction, convection and radiation that you would see at a campsite.

body.html: Conduction is energy transfer by particle collisions in contact; convection is transfer by the motion of a fluid; radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves (no matter needed).

Conduction: the handle of a metal pot warms where it touches the pot; a hot rock warms your hand. Convection: smoke and hot air rising above the fire, or water circulating as it heats in the pot. Radiation: the warmth you feel on your face from the fire, or sunlight warming the tent.

answer.html: Conduction: the metal pot handle heating up. Convection: hot air and smoke rising above the fire. Radiation: warmth from the fire reaching your face.

check.html: Only radiation can cross empty space, so it is the only one of the three that explains how sunlight warms the tent.

items.title: Figure 9 caption question: A teakettle has a copper bottom, a stainless steel body and a plastic knob on the lid. Explain how the choice of these materials is related to their specific heats and conductivity.

body.html: A low specific heat means a small energy input produces a large temperature rise ( 𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇). Metals also conduct heat well.

Copper (385 J/(kg · K)) has a low specific heat and conducts very well, so the base heats quickly and passes the energy to the water efficiently. Stainless steel is also a metal with a low specific heat, so the kettle body warms fast with little energy wasted. The plastic knob is a poor conductor, so it stays cool enough to touch. Water has a large specific heat (4180), so it warms much more slowly than the metal.

answer.html: The copper base and steel body are metals with low specific heats and good conductivity, so they heat quickly and pass energy to the water; the plastic knob conducts poorly, so it stays cool enough to hold.

check.html: An empty kettle heats up very fast, while one full of water heats up much more slowly, which matches the large difference in specific heats.

items.title: Get It? (energy transfer and transformation): Describe how energy is transferred and transformed when an electric kettle heats water.

body.html: Energy is conserved; it is transferred as heat and can change form.

Electrical energy is transformed into thermal energy in the heating element. The element transfers heat to the water touching it by conduction, and convection carries the energy through the water. The hot kettle and water then lose some energy to the room by conduction, convection and radiation, which is why the kettle eventually cools.

answer.html: Electrical energy becomes thermal energy in the heating element; it is conducted into the water, spread by convection, and partly lost to the room by conduction, convection and radiation.

check.html: Total energy in equals the energy gained by the water plus the energy lost to the surroundings.

body.html: equal masses 𝑚= 0.350 kg of the same substance; 𝑇<sub>𝐴</sub>= 65.0°C , 𝑇<sub>𝐵</sub>= 18.0°C. Find 𝑇<sub>𝑓</sub>.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Lesson 1 Problem 9: On a cold morning a metal park bench and a wooden park bench, which have been outside all night, are both at the air temperature. Is the metal bench colder than the wooden bench? Explain why the metal one feels colder.

body.html: Skin feels the rate of heat conduction, not the temperature itself.

Both benches have been in contact with the air all night, so they are in thermal equilibrium with it and are at the same temperature. Metal is a much better thermal conductor than wood, so it carries energy away from your warm hand faster, which makes it feel colder.

answer.html: No, both benches are at the same temperature as the air. The metal bench feels colder because it conducts thermal energy away from your hand faster than wood does.

check.html: A thermometer pressed on each bench would give the same reading.

items.title: 10: Convert each temperature. Use 𝑇𝐾= 𝑇𝐶+ 273. (a) 22°C to kelvins; (b)

question.html: 58 K to degrees Celsius; (c) 150°C to kelvins; (d) 400 K to degrees Celsius.

body.html: The Kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size degree but differ by an offset of 273: 𝑇<sub>𝐾</sub>= 𝑇<sub>𝐶</sub>+ 273 and 𝑇<sub>𝐶</sub>= 𝑇<sub>𝐾</sub>−273.

check.html: Kelvin values are never negative; (b) is very cold but above absolute zero (−273°C).

items.title: 11: A student writes 𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇. Which of the quantities 𝐶 and the product

question.html: 𝑚𝐶 has units of J/K? Give the units of each, and say whether 𝑄 has the same units as 𝐶.

body.html: 𝑄 is energy (joules). From 𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇, 𝐶= 𝑄/ (𝑚𝛥𝑇).

The unit of 𝐶 is J/(kg·K) . Multiplying by mass in kilograms cancels the kg, so 𝑚𝐶 has units of J/K (energy per kelvin: the energy needed to raise this particular object's temperature by 1 K). 𝑄 has units of joules.

answer.html: 𝐶 is in J/(kg·K) ; the product 𝑚𝐶 is in J/K; 𝑄 is in J. So 𝑄 and 𝐶 do not have the same units.

check.html: (J/K)(K) = J, so 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇 is in joules, as required for 𝑄.

items.title: 12: A tennis ball is dropped from a balcony onto concrete and bounces several times, each bounce lower than the one before. Describe the ball's mechanical and thermal energy during the motion.

body.html: Mechanical energy is the ball's gravitational potential plus kinetic energy; collisions convert some of it to thermal energy.

At the balcony, the ball has maximum gravitational potential energy and no kinetic energy. As it falls, PE becomes KE. At the concrete the ball is squashed and its energy is briefly stored as elastic potential energy. At each bounce some mechanical energy becomes thermal energy (the ball, the air inside it and the concrete warm slightly) and sound, so the ball rebounds to a lower height each time.

answer.html: Mechanical energy (PE + KE) trades back and forth during each bounce but decreases overall; the lost mechanical energy shows up as thermal energy (and sound) in the ball, air and concrete. Total energy is conserved.

check.html: The bounces get lower, so the mechanical energy must be going somewhere: into thermal energy.

items.title: 13: Could a small pot of boiling water have less thermal energy than a bathtub of lukewarm water? Explain.

body.html: Thermal energy depends on both temperature and the number of particles (mass).

Thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles. The boiling pot has a high average energy per particle but contains few particles. The bathtub has a lower average energy per particle but a huge number of particles, so its total can be far larger.

answer.html: Yes. The bathtub holds much more water (many more particles), so its total thermal energy can be greater than that of the small pot even though the pot has the higher temperature.

check.html: For equal masses of water, the hotter water would always have more thermal energy.

items.title: 14: Explain why a bowl of thick soup stays hot longer than a slice of toast taken from the oven at the same time and temperature.

body.html: The energy a hot object holds (𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇) and the rate it loses it depend on specific heat, mass, and conduction.

The soup is mostly water, which has a very high specific heat, so each kilogram holds a lot of thermal energy per degree, and there is much more mass in the bowl than in the toast. The toast is thin, has a low specific heat and a large surface area, so it holds little energy and loses it quickly to the air.

answer.html: The soup has a large specific heat (mostly water) and a large mass, so it stores a lot of thermal energy and releases it slowly; the thin toast stores little and loses it quickly.

check.html: A thin layer of soup spread on a plate would cool much faster than the bowlful.

items.title: 15: Why does a pile of crushed ice cool a drink faster than a single large ice cube of the same mass?

body.html: Heat enters the ice through its surface by conduction, and more surface means a faster transfer.

Thermal energy passes from the drink to the ice across the surface of the ice. Crushed ice has many small pieces, so its total surface area in contact with the drink is much larger than that of one large cube. Each small piece is also thin, so energy reaches its center quickly. A larger transfer rate means the drink cools and the ice melts faster.

answer.html: The crushed ice has far more surface area in contact with the liquid and shorter distances for energy to reach the center of each piece, so thermal energy is transferred faster than with the single large cube.

check.html: Same reasoning explains why sugar powder dissolves faster than a sugar cube.

items.title: 16: Why are computer chip heat sinks usually made of aluminum or copper rather than glass or plastic?

body.html: Metals have low specific heats and high conductivity, so they absorb energy readily and spread it.

A heat sink must move thermal energy away from the chip quickly. Aluminum and copper are good thermal conductors, so energy flows through them quickly from the chip into fins where air carries it away. Their low specific heats also mean they respond quickly to changes in energy. Glass and plastic conduct poorly and would trap the heat near the chip.

answer.html: Aluminum and copper are good thermal conductors with low specific heats, so they take thermal energy away from the chip quickly and pass it to the air.

check.html: A plastic cup of hot water stays hot to hold longer than a metal one, which shows poor conductors do the opposite job.

items.title: 17: A baked potato wrapped in aluminum foil comes out of the oven. The foil is at the same temperature as the potato, yet you can touch the foil for a moment but the potato burns your fingers. Explain.

body.html: Compare how much thermal energy each can deliver to your finger; 𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇.

The potato is mostly water (𝐶= 4180 J/(kg · K)) and has far more mass than the thin foil. When it cools against your finger, it releases far more energy. The thin foil has little mass and a lower specific heat (897 J/(kg · K)), so it holds little thermal energy and gives it up almost instantly, cooling to the temperature of your finger before it can burn you.

answer.html: The potato has a high specific heat and much more mass, so it holds and transfers much more thermal energy to your finger than the thin foil at the same temperature.

check.html: Same temperature does not mean the same thermal energy.

items.title: 18 (Critical Thinking): On a cold day you see a white cloud form when you exhale. What is the cloud made of, and why does it form?

body.html: Exhaled air contains water vapor; water vapor in cooler air condenses.

Your breath is warm and humid, so it carries water vapor (invisible). When it meets the cold air, it loses thermal energy and the vapor condenses into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets scatter light and appear as a white cloud. Thus the cloud is liquid water, not vapor.

answer.html: The water vapor in your breath condenses into tiny liquid droplets when it meets the cold air, and the droplets are the cloud we see.

check.html: The cloud vanishes a moment later as the droplets evaporate again into the surrounding air.

items.title: Figure 1 caption question, what do the arrows represent and why are they longer in the left balloon?

body.html: Particles in a gas move randomly. Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles.

Each arrow is a velocity vector of one gas particle: its length shows the speed and its direction shows the direction of motion. The left balloon is the hotter, fully inflated one, whose particles have greater average kinetic energy (𝐾𝐸=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup>) and so greater speeds, and so longer arrows.

answer.html: The arrows are velocity vectors of the gas particles (length = speed). They are longer in the left balloon because it is hotter, so its particles have a higher average kinetic energy and move faster.

check.html: The hotter, bigger balloon also has particles hitting the walls harder and more often, which is why it is more inflated.

items.title: Get It? (thermal equilibrium), an everyday example of an object and its surroundings moving toward equilibrium

body.html: Thermal energy flows spontaneously from hot to cold until the temperatures match.
A cup of hot cocoa left on a desk cools until it is at room temperature; the air warms by a tiny amount. An ice cube dropped in a drink warms and melts while the drink cools.

answer.html: Example: a mug of hot cocoa on a desk. Energy spreads from the cocoa into the cooler room until the cocoa and the room are at the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

check.html: In every example the hotter object cools and the cooler one warms, never the reverse.

items.title: Figure 5 caption question, summarize what happens when the liquid crystal thermometer is placed on a forehead

body.html: Conduction and thermal equilibrium (a thermometer reads its own temperature).

The forehead is warmer than the thermometer, so the skin's more energetic particles collide with the strip's particles and transfer energy to it by conduction. The strip warms until the energy transfer in each direction is equal, which is thermal equilibrium at the skin's temperature. The liquid-crystal molecules rearrange at specific temperatures and change color, so the color shown tells the temperature.

answer.html: Thermal energy is conducted from the warm forehead to the cooler strip until the two reach thermal equilibrium; the liquid crystals change color at that temperature, giving the reading.

check.html: The reading is only valid after waiting for equilibrium, which is why you hold a thermometer in place for a moment.

items.title: Get It? (alcohol thermometer), describe how an alcohol thermometer works

body.html: A thermometer uses a property that changes with temperature (here, volume of a liquid).

The bulb touches the object, and thermal energy flows until the alcohol is at the object's temperature. The warmer alcohol expands and rises up the narrow tube; the height at equilibrium is read against a scale.

answer.html: The alcohol reaches thermal equilibrium with the object, expands as its temperature rises, and rises in the tube; the height of the liquid column indicates the temperature.

check.html: A colder object makes the alcohol contract and the column drop, as expected.

items.title: Get It? (absolute zero), why "absolute zero" is an appropriate name

body.html: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles; the Kelvin scale starts where this energy is zero.

At −273.15°C all the thermal energy that can be removed has been removed, the particles are essentially motionless, and the temperature cannot be lowered further. A temperature below that would require negative kinetic energy, which is impossible.

answer.html: It is the absolute lowest possible temperature (0 K): the particles have no kinetic energy left to give up, so nothing can be colder, and the Kelvin scale starts there with no negative values.

check.html: 0 K = −273.15°C, the value the book gives.

items.title: Figure 8 caption question, other common examples of conduction, convection, and radiation

body.html: Conduction is energy transfer by particle collisions in contact; convection is transfer by the motion of a fluid; radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves (no matter needed).

Conduction: a metal spoon warming in hot soup, a hot pan handle, your hand on an ice cube. Convection: warm air rising above a radiator or heater, boiling water circulating, sea breezes, ocean currents. Radiation: a campfire warming your face, a heat lamp, a microwave oven cooking food, the Sun warming Earth.

answer.html: Conduction: spoon in hot soup. Convection: warm air rising from a heater. Radiation: warmth from a campfire or the Sun.

check.html: Only radiation can cross a vacuum, which is how the Sun's energy reaches Earth.

items.title: Figure 9 caption question, explain how the pan materials relate to their specific heats

body.html: A low specific heat means a small energy input produces a large temperature rise ( 𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇). Metals also conduct well.

Copper (385 J/(kg · K)) and stainless steel have low specific heats and conduct well, so the pan bottom heats up quickly and spreads the energy evenly to the food. The plastic handle is a poor conductor, so it stays cool enough to hold. Water in the food has a high specific heat, so the food heats more slowly than the pan.

answer.html: The pan body and copper base are metals with low specific heats and good conductivity, so they heat quickly and evenly; the plastic handle conducts poorly so it stays cool to touch.

check.html: This matches experience: an empty metal pan gets hot very fast, a pan of water much more slowly.

items.title: Get It? (cup of liquid on the first page), how is energy transferred and transformed?

body.html: Energy is conserved; it is transferred as heat and can change form.

Chemical energy in the fuel (or electrical energy in the burner) is transformed to thermal energy of the burner. The burner transfers heat to the pot by conduction/radiation, the pot conducts it to the liquid, and convection carries it through the liquid. The hot pot and liquid then radiate infrared (seen by the camera) and lose energy to the air by convection and conduction.

answer.html: Chemical (or electrical) energy becomes thermal energy at the burner; it is transferred by conduction into the pot and liquid, spread by convection, and lost to the surroundings by radiation and convection.

check.html: Total energy in equals the energy stored in the liquid plus the energy lost to the surroundings.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Lesson 1 Problem 9, Bathroom tile floor

question.html: Is the tile floor colder than the rest of the room? Explain.

body.html: Skin feels the rate of heat conduction, not the temperature itself.

The floor and the room have been in contact long enough to be at the same temperature (thermal equilibrium). Tile is a good thermal conductor compared with a rug or wood, so it carries energy away from your warm foot faster, which makes it feel cold.

answer.html: No, the floor is at the same temperature as the rest of the room. It feels colder because tile conducts thermal energy away from your feet faster than other materials.

check.html: A thermometer on the tile would read the same as the room's air.

items.title: 11, Units of heat and specific heat

question.html: Are the units of 𝑄 and 𝐶 the same?

body.html: 𝑄 is energy (joules). From 𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇, 𝐶= 𝑄/ (𝑚𝛥𝑇).
The unit of 𝐶 is J/(kg·K) , joules per kilogram per kelvin.

answer.html: No. Heat 𝑄 is in joules (J); specific heat 𝐶 is in J/(kg·K) because it is the energy needed per kilogram per kelvin.

check.html: Multiplying 𝐶 by 𝑚 (kg) and 𝛥𝑇 (K) gives joules, as required.

items.title: 12, Bouncing basketball

question.html: Describe the mechanical and thermal energy of a bouncing basketball.

body.html: Mechanical energy is the ball's gravitational potential plus kinetic energy; collisions convert some of it to thermal energy.

Held at the top, the ball has maximum gravitational potential energy and no kinetic energy. Falling, it converts PE to KE. At the floor it is compressed and its energy is briefly elastic potential energy. In each bounce some mechanical energy becomes thermal energy (the ball, the air inside and the floor warm slightly) and sound, so it rebounds lower each time.

answer.html: Mechanical energy (PE + KE) trades back and forth during each bounce but decreases overall; the lost mechanical energy shows up as thermal energy (and sound), warming the ball, air and floor slightly. Total energy is conserved.

check.html: Each bounce is lower, so the mechanical energy must be going somewhere: into thermal energy.

items.title: 13, Equal thermal energy for hot and cold water?

question.html: Could the thermal energy of a bowl of hot water equal that of a bowl of cold water?

body.html: Thermal energy depends on both temperature and the number of particles (mass).

A small bowl of hot water and a much larger bowl of cold water can contain the same total thermal energy: fewer particles with high average energy can add up to the same total as many particles with lower average energy (like the two muffins in Figure 3, in reverse).

answer.html: Yes. If the cold water has enough more mass (more particles) than the hot water, the totals can be equal even though the hot water has the higher temperature.

check.html: For equal masses of water, the hot bowl would always have more thermal energy.

items.title: 14, Baked potato stays hot longest

body.html: The energy a hot object holds (𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇) and the rate it loses it depend on specific heat, mass, and conduction.

A potato is mostly water, which has a very high specific heat, so each kilogram holds a lot of thermal energy per degree. It also is thick and conducts heat poorly, so energy leaves slowly. It cools off more slowly than thin or metallic foods.

answer.html: A potato has a large specific heat (mostly water) and a large mass, so it stores a lot of thermal energy and, being a poor conductor, releases it slowly.

check.html: Compare a thin slice of the same potato: it would cool quickly.

items.title: 15, Whole potato versus cut potato

body.html: Heat reaches the center of food by conduction from the surface.

A whole potato has a long path from the hot surface to its center, and potato conducts heat poorly, so the center warms slowly. Cutting it into pieces gives each piece a short path and a larger total surface area exposed to the hot oven air, so the energy reaches all parts quickly.

answer.html: Pieces have more surface area exposed to heat and a shorter distance for energy to conduct to the center, so they cook faster than a whole potato.

check.html: Same reasoning explains why thin pancakes cook faster than thick ones.

items.title: 16, Metals for stovetop pans

body.html: Low specific heat (heats quickly) and high conductivity (spreads heat).
Copper, iron and aluminum are good thermal conductors with relatively low specific heats, so they transfer energy from the burner to the food efficiently and heat up quickly with little energy.

answer.html: They are good thermal conductors with low specific heats, so they heat quickly and evenly and transfer the heat to the food.

check.html: Handles are made of other materials because they should be poor conductors.

items.title: 17, Plastic spoon versus hot cocoa

body.html: Compare how much thermal energy each can deliver to your tongue; the cocoa is mostly water with a large specific heat and much more mass.

The cocoa is at the same temperature as the spoon but is mostly water ( 𝐶= 4180 J/(kg · K)) and has far more mass. When it cools on your tongue, it releases far more energy (𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇). The thin plastic spoon has little mass and a lower specific heat, so it contains little thermal energy and gives it up quickly.

answer.html: The cocoa has a high specific heat and much more mass, so it holds and transfers much more thermal energy to your tongue than the small plastic spoon at the same temperature.

check.html: Same temperature does not mean same thermal energy (Figure 3, muffins).

items.title: 18 (Critical Thinking), Mist above heating water

body.html: Water at the surface evaporates; water vapor near cooler air condenses.

Hot water gives off water vapor (invisible). Just above the surface the vapor meets cooler air and loses energy, condensing into tiny liquid droplets, which scatter light and appear as mist. Thus the mist is liquid water, not vapor.

answer.html: Water vapor leaving the hot surface condenses into tiny liquid droplets in the cooler air above the pot, which we see as mist.

check.html: The mist disappears again higher up as the droplets re-evaporate in drier air.
